General Principles.title: General Principles of Radiation Oncology
General Principles.html:
Radiation oncology is the medical specialty that uses carefully targeted, high-energy radiation to destroy cancer cells (and occasionally to treat certain non-cancerous conditions). It is one of three pillars of cancer treatment, and understanding how it fits alongside the other two, and the vocabulary oncologists use to describe treatment goals, is the foundation for everything else in this rotation.

The Multidisciplinary Approach to Cancer

Almost no cancer is treated by a single specialist working alone. Cancer care is built around three complementary specialties, each contributing a different kind of therapy:

  • Medical oncology delivers systemic therapy: treatment that travels throughout the whole body, such as chemotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, and hormone therapy. Systemic therapy is used because cancer cells (or micrometastatic disease) can be anywhere in the body, not just at the primary site.
  • Surgical oncology delivers local therapy: physically resecting the tumor, sampling or removing lymph nodes, or performing palliative debulking to relieve symptoms from bulky disease.
  • Radiation oncology also delivers local (or regional) therapy, but does so with beams of radiation or radioactive sources rather than a scalpel. Radiation can be used with curative intent, palliative intent, or to control oligometastatic disease (a small number of metastases).

Because these three specialties treat the same patient with different tools, most cancer patients are seen at a multidisciplinary consultation where the team collectively decides on a treatment sequence.

The Language of Treatment Intent

Every treatment plan is described using a small set of intent-related terms. Learning these precisely matters because they change how aggressive treatment is, and in what order therapies are given.

  • Curative: the explicit goal is to eliminate the cancer.
  • Palliative: the goal is not cure but relief of symptoms (pain, bleeding, obstruction, etc.) in the setting of incurable disease.
  • Definitive: this treatment is intended to be the final, complete treatment, no further therapy is planned afterward.
  • Neoadjuvant: therapy given first, before the primary (usually definitive) treatment, for example, shrinking a tumor before surgery.
  • Adjuvant: additional therapy given after the primary treatment, typically to reduce the risk of recurrence by eliminating microscopic residual disease.
  • Concurrent: two treatments given at the same time, most classically concurrent chemoradiation, where chemotherapy is used to radiosensitize the tumor while radiation is delivered.

These terms combine freely, a patient might receive neoadjuvant chemotherapy, then definitive concurrent chemoradiation, for instance, so always ask "what is the intent of THIS specific treatment?" rather than assuming intent applies to the whole care plan.

The General Workup: From Diagnosis to Follow-Up

Nearly every new cancer patient moves through the same four-step framework:

  • Diagnosis: the patient presents with a chief complaint; history, physical exam, and imaging raise suspicion, and a biopsy ultimately provides the tissue diagnosis.
  • Staging: additional imaging and sometimes surgical staging procedures determine the anatomic extent of disease, typically summarized using the TNM system (tumor size/extent, lymph node involvement, distant metastasis) and translated into an overall group stage (I–IV).
  • Treatment: the team defines whether the goal is curative or palliative, then holds multidisciplinary consultation to sequence therapies.
  • Follow-up: patients are monitored for treatment toxicity and undergo periodic exams and restaging imaging to watch for recurrence.

Performance status (a standardized measure of how well a patient can carry out daily activities) is assessed throughout this entire process, since it influences how aggressively a patient can be treated.

Clinical PearlFor essentially every new radiation oncology patient, build the habit of screening for a short list of "do not forget" issues: smoking cessation counseling, fertility counseling before any treatment that could affect the gonads, a pregnancy test in anyone of childbearing potential, and genetic counseling when the history suggests a hereditary cancer syndrome.

When Is Radiation Used?

Radiation is not reserved for any single stage of cancer, it has a role across the entire spectrum of disease:

  • Curative (definitive): radiation alone, or chemoradiation, can cure cancer outright in sites such as head & neck, lung, prostate, anal, and cervical cancer.
  • Adjuvant: radiation (with or without chemotherapy) is given after surgery to reduce recurrence risk in cancers such as glioma/glioblastoma, breast, pancreas, and sarcoma.
  • Palliative: in metastatic or otherwise incurable disease, radiation rapidly relieves symptoms, treating painful bone metastases, spinal cord compression from vertebral metastases, SVC syndrome, airway obstruction or hemoptysis, and GI or pelvic bleeding.
  • Oligometastatic disease: when a patient has only a few sites of metastatic or progressing disease, focused radiation (often SRS/SBRT) can be used to "consolidate" or locally control those spots, sometimes delaying the need to change systemic therapy.

Radiation also treats a range of benign conditions: meningioma, acoustic neuroma, trigeminal neuralgia, tremor (via thalamic ablation), keloids, Dupuytren's contracture, and prophylaxis against heterotopic ossification.

Example Treatment Paradigms

Two worked examples illustrate how these principles come together in practice.

Glioblastoma (GBM), the most common malignant primary brain tumor in adults, is treated with a well-defined sequence: upfront maximal safe surgical resection, followed by concurrent chemoradiation for up to six weeks (daily oral temozolomide during radiation), followed by adjuvant chemotherapy with temozolomide for six to twelve months (days 1–5 of every four-week cycle).

Stage III non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), where tumor has spread to mediastinal lymph nodes but is not yet metastatic, is treated with concurrent chemoradiation (typically carboplatin plus paclitaxel, or carboplatin plus pemetrexed) followed by adjuvant immunotherapy with durvalumab. Notice the pattern in both examples: local therapy (surgery and/or radiation) is paired with systemic therapy, sequenced deliberately around the local treatment.

Radiation Delivery & Technique.title: Radiation Delivery and Treatment Techniques
Radiation Delivery & Technique.html:
Once a cancer team decides that radiation should be part of a patient's treatment, the next question is how to physically deliver it. Radiation can be delivered from a machine outside the body, or from a radioactive source placed inside or next to the tumor, and within each of those broad categories, there is a whole toolkit of techniques that trade off complexity, precision, and treatment time.

EBRT vs. Brachytherapy: Two Fundamentally Different Approaches

External beam radiation therapy (EBRT) uses a machine positioned outside the patient's body to aim a beam of photons, electrons, or particles (like protons) through the skin and into the target. It is by far the most common form of radiation delivery, and photon EBRT is used more often than any other modality.

Brachytherapy (BT) instead places a radioactive source directly inside the body, inside a body cavity (intracavitary), inside the tumor itself (interstitial), or immediately adjacent to it. Because the source sits right next to (or inside) the target, brachytherapy can deliver a very high dose to the tumor while the dose falls off extremely quickly with distance, sparing nearby normal tissue. Classic examples include prostate seed implants and intracavitary treatment of cervical cancer.

How a LINAC Produces Its Beam

The workhorse machine of modern EBRT is the linear accelerator (LINAC). Inside the LINAC head, electrons are accelerated to high energy (typically in the range of 6-18 MeV) and steered into a heavy metal (tungsten) target. When these fast electrons interact with the target's nucleus, they undergo Bremsstrahlung ("braking radiation"): they are rapidly decelerated, and the energy they lose is emitted as high-energy photons. This is the same basic process, on a much larger scale, that produces diagnostic X-rays. The resulting photon beam then passes through a flattening filter (to make the beam intensity uniform across its width) and is shaped by jaws and multi-leaf collimators (MLCs), banks of individually-moving metal leaves, before reaching the patient. The same LINAC can also deliver electron therapy: the tungsten target and flattening filter are swapped out for a scattering foil, and an electron applicator (cone) shapes the beam, making electrons well suited for treating superficial tumors near the skin surface. The gantry housing the head can rotate around the patient, allowing treatment from many angles.

From 2D to VMAT: Increasing Conformality

Radiation techniques have evolved to sculpt dose more and more precisely around the tumor while sparing surrounding organs at risk (OAR):

  • Conventional (2D) RT: simple setups using 2-4 fields, planned using basic anatomic landmarks rather than full 3D imaging.
  • 3D conformal RT (3DCRT): uses CT-based 3D imaging to contour the target and surrounding OARs, allowing more fields and better shaping of the dose to the tumor's actual geometry.
  • Intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT): goes a step further by varying the intensity of radiation across each individual beam (rather than delivering a uniform beam), producing highly conformal dose distributions that can even wrap dose around a critical structure. IMRT can be delivered as segmental ("step-and-shoot") IMRT, where the MLCs move into position and then hold still while the beam is on, or dynamic IMRT, where the MLC leaves are in continuous motion throughout treatment of each field.
  • Volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT): delivers radiation continuously as the gantry rotates around the patient in an arc, with the MLCs dynamically modulating the beam throughout, combining the conformality of IMRT with much faster delivery times.

Stereotactic Techniques: SRS and SBRT

Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) and stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) are highly targeted techniques that deliver a very high dose per fraction over just one to five total fractions ("ultra-hypofractionation"), relying on extremely precise setup and imaging to safely concentrate dose into a small volume. By convention, SRS refers to stereotactic treatment of brain tumors (delivered with systems such as GammaKnife or CyberKnife), while SBRT refers to the same general approach applied to tumors elsewhere in the body (lung, liver, spine, etc.).

Brachytherapy: LDR vs. HDR

Brachytherapy is further divided by how quickly the radioactive source delivers its dose:

  • Low-dose-rate (LDR) brachytherapy: radioactive sources (such as permanent seeds) are implanted in a single procedure, for example prostate seed implants, and then deliver their dose slowly over an extended period as they decay.
  • High-dose-rate (HDR) brachytherapy: an applicator is placed inside the patient, and a radioactive source is then delivered through the applicator on a wire from a machine called an afterloader for just a few minutes at a time, then withdrawn, a classic example is intracavitary tandem-based treatment of cervical cancer.
Clinical PearlA quick way to keep these techniques straight: 2D and 3DCRT use uniform-intensity beams from a small number of fixed angles; IMRT modulates the intensity within each beam for better conformality; VMAT modulates intensity continuously while the gantry rotates, trading some conformality for much faster treatment times; and SRS/SBRT compress an entire, highly conformal treatment course into just one to five fractions.

Craniospinal Irradiation: A Technique Case Study

Craniospinal irradiation (CSI) treats the entire brain and spinal subarachnoid space, and is used for tumors that can spread through the cerebrospinal fluid, for example pediatric medulloblastoma, non-germinomatous germ cell tumors, atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumor (ATRT), and metastatic ependymoma, as well as leptomeningeal disease from adult cancers such as breast cancer. CSI illustrates several delivery concepts at once: it typically requires two to three separate isocenters (opposed lateral fields for the whole brain, plus one or more posterior fields for the spine), and because each field naturally diverges (its diameter increases with distance from the source), the fields must be carefully matched, by rotating the collimator and kicking the treatment couch, to avoid creating dangerous hot spots where fields overlap. When multiple spine fields are needed, the match line is deliberately shifted every few fractions, a technique called "feathering the junction," which spreads out the unavoidable cold spot over a larger area of normal tissue rather than concentrating it in one place.

Radiation Physics.title: Radiation Physics Fundamentals
Radiation Physics.html:
Radiation physics explains what actually happens, at the level of photons, electrons, and atoms, when a beam passes through the body, and it is the reason different beam types (photons, electrons, protons) behave so differently in tissue. Understanding these mechanisms is what lets a radiation oncologist choose the right beam, and the right energy, for a given tumor.

Photon Interactions with Matter

A photon is a massless packet of energy that travels at the speed of light. As photons pass through matter, they can interact in four main ways, and which interaction dominates depends on the photon's energy and the atomic number (Z) of the material it hits:

InteractionWhat happensDepends on / occurs at
Coherent scatteringElastic scattering; the photon changes direction but loses no energy (not enough energy to eject an electron)Very low photon energies
Photoelectric effectPhoton transfers ALL its energy to an inner-shell electron, ejecting it; an outer-shell electron fills the vacancy, releasing a characteristic X-ray or Auger electronLow energies; probability ∝ Z³/E³ (drives diagnostic imaging contrast)
Compton scatteringPhoton transfers SOME energy to an outer-shell electron, ejecting it, then continues on as a lower-energy scattered photonTherapeutic energies (roughly 25 keV-25 MeV); depends on electron density, nearly independent of Z
Pair productionPhoton interacts with the nucleus and converts into an electron-positron pairRequires ≥1.022 MeV; only a real concern above about 10 MV

At the energies used for therapeutic photon beams, Compton scattering dominates. This matters clinically because Compton interactions depend on electron density rather than atomic number, which is part of why photon dose deposition is relatively predictable across different soft tissues.

How LINACs Generate Photons: Bremsstrahlung

Photon beams for treatment are generated when a LINAC accelerates electrons and directs them into a tungsten target (a high-Z material). As each electron passes near a tungsten nucleus, it is deflected and rapidly decelerated, this "braking" interaction is called Bremsstrahlung, and the electron's lost kinetic energy is emitted as an X-ray photon. This process is inefficient (only about a third of the electron energy becomes usable X-rays), and critically, the resulting photon beam is polyenergetic: it contains a spectrum of photon energies up to the maximum electron energy, with an average energy roughly one-third to one-half of that maximum.

The Percent Depth Dose (PDD) Curve

The percent depth dose (PDD) curve describes how a beam's dose changes with depth in tissue, and its shape is one of the most clinically important physics concepts to internalize.

For photon beams, dose does not peak at the skin. Instead, it takes some depth of tissue before enough high-speed electrons have been ejected by photon interactions to build up to a maximum, this shallow region is called the buildup region, and the depth at which dose peaks is called Dmax. Beyond Dmax, the beam gradually loses dose to attenuation and scatter, but because photons pass essentially all the way through the body, there is always some exit dose on the far side. Higher-energy photon beams have a deeper Dmax and a lower surface dose, a rough rule of thumb is that Dmax (in cm) equals beam energy (in MV) divided by 4 for energies up to 10 MV, and divided by 5 for energies of 15 MV and above (for example, Co-60 is about 0.5 cm, 6 MV about 1.5 cm, 10 MV about 2.5 cm, 15 MV about 3 cm, and 18 MV about 3.5 cm).

Electron beams behave in the opposite way at the surface: because electrons are charged particles that begin interacting immediately, surface dose is HIGHER (not lower) for higher-energy electron beams, and just like photons, higher energy pushes Dmax deeper. The key clinical difference is what happens after Dmax, electron dose falls off very steeply once past a certain depth (the beam's practical range), so there is essentially no dose delivered beyond that depth. This is what makes electrons useful for superficial tumors: you can deliver a therapeutic dose to a shallow target while sparing whatever lies underneath.

A convenient way to estimate an electron beam's depth-dose landmarks is the "5-4-3-2" rule of thumb, where E is the electron energy in MeV: Dmax ≈ E/5; the 90% isodose line (depth to which clinicians typically prescribe) ≈ E/3.2-3.3; the 80% isodose line ≈ E/2.8; and the practical range ≈ E/2. For example, a 9 MeV electron beam has a Dmax of about 4.5 cm and a practical range of about 4.5 cm, with the 90% isodose line around 2.8 cm deep.

Proton beams behave differently still. As a proton travels through tissue it continuously loses energy, but it deposits relatively little dose along most of its path, then, at the exact depth where it finally runs out of energy and stops, it deposits the majority of its dose all at once. This sharp spike is called the Bragg peak, and beyond it, dose drops essentially to zero, protons have no meaningful exit dose. A single-energy proton beam produces a narrow ("pristine") Bragg peak; in practice, beams of multiple energies are combined to create a spread-out Bragg peak (SOBP) that covers the full thickness of a tumor.

Translating Physics into Beam Selection

These PDD shapes are exactly why beam choice is a clinical decision, not just a technical one. A superficial skin lesion a few centimeters deep is an excellent electron target, you pick an energy whose 90% isodose line covers the depth of the lesion, so the dose falls off before reaching deeper structures. A deep-seated tumor (most solid organ cancers) needs photons, which can reach depth while still sparing some dose to the entrance and exit paths, especially when multiple beam angles are combined. When sparing tissue distal to (behind) the target is the top priority, for example, sparing the growing brain or heart in a child, or the tissue beyond a target that sits near critical structures, protons offer a real advantage because of the sharp Bragg peak and lack of exit dose, at the cost of being more sensitive to daily setup and anatomic uncertainty.

Clinical PearlRemember the surface-dose paradox: for photons, HIGHER energy means LOWER surface dose and a DEEPER Dmax. For electrons, HIGHER energy means HIGHER surface dose (as well as a deeper Dmax). Mixing these up is one of the most common physics exam errors.

Radiation Biology.title: Radiation Biology Fundamentals
Radiation Biology.html:
Radiation biology explains why radiation kills cells at all, and why splitting a total radiation dose into many small daily treatments (fractionation) is more effective and safer than delivering it all at once. These principles connect the physics of radiation directly to the clinical practice of prescribing daily treatments over several weeks.

How Radiation Kills Cells: Direct and Indirect Action

Radiation is energy, either electromagnetic waves (x-rays, gamma rays) or particles (electrons, protons, alpha particles, neutrons), and it is ionizing, meaning it has enough energy to eject electrons from atoms. Charged particles (electrons, protons, alpha particles) are directly ionizing: they pass through tissue and directly produce chemical and biologic damage. Electromagnetic waves and neutrons are indirectly ionizing: they are absorbed and give up their energy to produce fast-moving charged particles (x-rays and gamma rays produce fast electrons), which then cause the actual damage.

Radiation's most important biological target is DNA, and it can damage DNA in two ways. Direct action occurs when radiation ionizes the DNA molecule itself. Indirect action, the dominant mechanism for x-rays and gamma rays, occurs when radiation ionizes nearby water molecules, generating highly reactive free radicals that then diffuse a very short distance and damage DNA chemically. Because oxygen helps stabilize (or "fix") this free-radical damage into a permanent chemical change, the presence of oxygen is a major determinant of how effective a given dose of radiation will be (see OER, below).

DNA Damage and Repair

A dose of just 1 Gy of radiation produces roughly 1,000 single-strand breaks (SSBs) in a cell's DNA and about 40 double-strand breaks (DSBs). SSBs are generally not lethal on their own and are efficiently repaired by pathways including base excision repair (BER), nucleotide excision repair (NER), and mismatch repair (MMR) (which corrects DNA replication errors rather than radiation damage per se). DSBs are the critical lesion: they are the hardest type of damage to repair accurately, and if unrepaired or misrepaired, they lead to lethal chromosome and chromatid aberrations (dicentrics, rings, anaphase bridges) that kill the cell when it attempts to divide.

DSBs are repaired by two competing pathways. Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) does not require an intact template, so it can act at any point in the cell cycle (including G1), fast but relatively error-prone. Homologous recombination (HR) requires an undamaged sister chromatid as a template, so it is only available in late S/G2 after DNA replication, slower but far more accurate. A DSB recruits the MRN complex, which activates ATM; ATM phosphorylates histone H2AX (forming γ-H2AX, a marker detectable within 15 minutes) and halts the cell cycle (via CHK2) to buy time for repair. 53BP1 promotes NHEJ, while BRCA1 promotes HR.

This machinery has direct clinical relevance: inherited defects cause recognizable syndromes with increased radiosensitivity and/or cancer risk, ataxia telangiectasia (ATM), Lynch syndrome (MMR genes), SCID/LIG4 deficiency (NHEJ genes), BRCA1/2 mutations (HR), and Fanconi anemia (crosslink repair). BRCA-associated HR deficiency is also the rationale for using PARP inhibitors (which impair BER) in BRCA-mutant cancers, making cells doubly dependent on the already-defective HR pathway.

Radiosensitivity Across the Cell Cycle

A cell's ability to survive radiation damage depends heavily on what phase of the cell cycle it is in. Cells are most sensitive to radiation in M phase (mitosis), and most resistant in late S/G2, because DNA has already been replicated and an intact copy is available as a repair template for accurate homologous recombination.

The Four R's of Radiobiology: Why We Fractionate

If radiation is so effective at killing cells, why not deliver the entire dose in one treatment? The answer is the four R's of radiobiology, which together explain why splitting treatment into daily fractions over several weeks improves the therapeutic ratio (kills more tumor while sparing more normal tissue):

  • Repair: normal tissue cells and cancer cells differ in their capacity to repair sublethal damage between fractions; fractionation gives normal tissue time to heal, reducing toxicity.
  • Repopulation: both normal and tumor tissue can increase their replication rate to replace cells lost to radiation; healthy tissue (like skin) that regenerates quickly benefits from this during a fractionated course.
  • Redistribution: after each fraction, radiosensitive cells (in M phase) are preferentially killed. In the interval before the next fraction, surviving cells move ("redistribute") through the cell cycle, so a new group of cells reaches the sensitive M phase before the next treatment, increasing the fraction of cells caught while vulnerable over the whole course.
  • Reoxygenation: as the more oxygenated (and more radiosensitive) tumor cells are killed off by early fractions, previously hypoxic tumor cells become closer to blood supply and reoxygenate, becoming more sensitive to subsequent fractions.

OER, LET, and RBE: Radiation Quality Matters

Not all radiation is equally effective per unit dose, and three linked concepts capture this. The oxygen enhancement ratio (OER) compares the dose needed for the same biologic effect under hypoxic versus aerobic conditions, about 2.5-3 for sparsely ionizing radiation like x-rays, lower (~1.6) for neutrons, and essentially 1 (no oxygen effect) for densely ionizing alpha particles. Linear energy transfer (LET) describes how densely a particle deposits energy along its track (keV/µm), x-rays and gamma rays are low-LET; neutrons and alpha particles are high-LET. As LET rises, OER falls, because densely ionizing radiation damages DNA directly, without needing oxygen to "fix" free-radical damage. Relative biological effectiveness (RBE) compares the dose of reference 250 kV x-rays to the dose of another radiation type needed for the same effect; RBE rises with increasing LET up to about 100 keV/µm (the ionization spacing that best matches the DNA double helix) and then falls beyond that, as extra ionizations are "wasted." Clinically, protons are assigned a fixed RBE of 1.1 relative to photons.

Why Fractionation Matters: The α/β Ratio, BED, and EQD2

The four R's explain qualitatively why fractionation helps; the α/β ratio is the quantitative tool that predicts how a specific tissue will respond to changes in fraction size. Cell killing from a single dose has a linear component (α, killing from a single "hit") and a quadratic component (β, killing from an accumulation of two "hits"); the α/β ratio is the dose at which these two components contribute equally. Early-responding tissues (skin, intestinal mucosa, bone marrow, and most tumors) have a HIGH α/β ratio (around 10) and are relatively insensitive to how the dose is split into fractions. Late-responding tissues (spinal cord, lung, kidney, liver, bladder, α/β around 3, with spinal cord often treated even more conservatively at around 2) have a LOW α/β ratio and are much more sensitive to the SIZE of each fraction, which is why large hypofractionated doses near these organs demand extra caution.

To compare regimens that use different fraction sizes, radiation oncologists use two related calculations. The biologically effective dose (BED): BED = nd[1 + d/(α/β)], where n is the number of fractions and d is the dose per fraction, converts any fractionation scheme into a single number that reflects its true biologic potency for a tissue of a given α/β. The equivalent dose in 2 Gy fractions (EQD2) converts that same regimen into "how many Gy would this be if given in standard 2 Gy fractions," which makes it easy to compare an unfamiliar hypofractionated regimen against familiar conventional dosing (and against published normal-tissue dose limits, which are usually reported in EQD2 or assume 2 Gy fractions).

Radiation toxicity itself is split into two categories that map onto these same tissue types. Acute toxicity is characterized by inflammation and is primarily a function of total dose, showing up during or shortly after treatment in rapidly-dividing early-responding tissues. Late toxicity is characterized by fibrosis and sclerosis, is primarily a function of dose PER FRACTION (which is why BED is used to estimate late-toxicity risk), and can appear months to years after treatment in late-responding tissues. The overarching goal of any fractionation scheme is to maximize the tumor control probability (TCP) while minimizing the normal tissue complication probability (NTCP): in other words, to widen the gap between the dose that controls the cancer and the dose that injures the patient.

Clinical PearlBecause late-responding tissues (low α/β) are disproportionately sensitive to fraction size, hypofractionation (fewer, larger fractions) must be used cautiously near organs like the spinal cord, while early-responding tissues and most tumors (high α/β) are comparatively more sensitive to total dose than to how it is split up.

Common Dose Constraints.title: Common Dose Constraints in Radiation Oncology
Common Dose Constraints.html:
A radiation prescription is not just about delivering enough dose to control the tumor, it is equally about staying under the dose that nearby healthy organs can tolerate. Dose constraints are the numeric limits placed on organs at risk (OAR) during planning, and they exist because radiation toxicity is often irreversible, so preventing it during planning is far better than treating it afterward.

Why Constraints Depend on Organ Architecture: Series vs. Parallel Organs

Not all organs fail the same way when part of them is damaged, and radiation oncology borrows an electrical-circuit analogy to describe this. Think of an organ's functional subunits as either wired in series or in parallel:

In a series organ, the subunits function like links in a chain, damage any single link severely enough, and the whole structure fails. For these organs, toxicity is driven by the maximum point dose anywhere in the organ, no matter how small that region is. Classic series organs include the spinal cord, brainstem, optic nerves, and bowel. In a parallel organ, subunits work independently side by side, so damaging some of them still leaves enough functioning tissue to preserve overall organ function. For these organs, toxicity is driven by the volume or mean dose received, not by any single hot spot. Classic parallel organs include the lung, liver, kidney, and parotid gland. This distinction is the single most important concept for interpreting any dose constraint table, always ask whether you are looking at a series organ (worry about the maximum) or a parallel organ (worry about the volume/mean).

The Language of Dose-Volume Constraints

Dose constraints are written in a compact shorthand that combines a dose and a volume (or vice versa). Learning to read this notation is essential:

  • V50% < 50%: the volume receiving 50% of the prescription dose or more should be less than 50% of the organ.
  • V15 Gy < 50%: the volume receiving 15 Gy or more should be less than 50% of the organ.
  • Dmax (or D0.03cc) ≤ 110%: the maximum point dose, often approximated using the dose to a small 0.03 cc voxel, since a true mathematical point has no volume, should be no more than 110% of prescription.
  • D90% ≥ 100%: the dose received by 90% of the target volume should be at least 100% of prescription (this kind of constraint is used to describe adequate target coverage, not just OAR sparing).

Radiation dose to any organ depends on total dose, dose per fraction, the tissue's α/β ratio, and total treatment time; constraints are typically quoted assuming conventional fractionation (2 Gy per fraction), and the biologically effective dose (BED) or EQD2 framework can be used to translate an unconventional fractionation schedule back into an equivalent conventional-fraction dose for comparison against these published limits.

QUANTEC: Constraints for Conventional Fractionation

The QUANTEC guidelines summarize widely-used normal-tissue dose constraints for conventionally fractionated radiation (2 Gy per fraction), each paired with an associated risk of a defined toxicity:

Notice the pattern: series organs (brain, brainstem, optic apparatus, spinal cord, stomach) are constrained by a maximum dose, while parallel organs (lung, parotid, kidney) are constrained by a volume (V) or mean dose, directly reflecting the series-vs-parallel architecture discussed above. For the spinal cord specifically, risk of myelopathy rises steeply with total dose (at 2 Gy/fraction): about 0.2% at 50 Gy, 6% at 60 Gy, and 50% at 69 Gy, which is exactly why 50 Gy is the conventional constraint.

HYTEC: Constraints for SRS/SBRT

Because SRS/SBRT delivers much higher doses per fraction over only 1-5 fractions, conventional QUANTEC limits do not directly apply, the HYTEC guidelines provide separate constraints for hypofractionated/ablative regimens. For example, spinal cord dose limits for a 1-5% risk of myelopathy rise with the number of fractions used:

Clinical PearlAlways match the reference (QUANTEC vs. HYTEC) to the fractionation being used, QUANTEC numbers assume roughly 2 Gy/fraction, and applying them directly to a 1-5 fraction SBRT/SRS course will give a badly wrong answer. When comparing across fractionation schemes, convert doses using EQD2/BED rather than comparing raw total Gy.
Clinical PearlWhen you see a constraint written as "Vx < y%" or "Vx Gy < y%," it is always describing a parallel-organ, volume-based limit; when you see "Dmax" or "D0.03cc," it is describing a series-organ, point-dose limit. Recognizing the format instantly tells you which type of organ you are protecting.

Acronyms & Terminology.title: Rad Onc Acronyms and Terminology
Acronyms & Terminology.html:
Radiation oncology runs on a dense vocabulary of acronyms, and a new learner can feel completely lost in a chart note or tumor board that is 80% abbreviations. The good news is that almost every acronym maps onto one predictable framework: the patient's journey through a course of radiation, from simulation, to planning, to plan review, to treatment, to follow-up. Grouping the jargon by where it belongs in that journey makes it far easier to remember.

Simulation: Capturing the Patient's Position and Motion

Simulation ("Sim") is the process of imaging the patient in their exact treatment position, most often using a CT Sim (CT scan performed with the patient immobilized and set up exactly as they will be for daily treatment). An isocenter ("Iso") is established, a fixed reference point in space that the treatment machine will target every day. Because tumors near the diaphragm or chest wall move with breathing, a 4D motion study may be performed (a CT acquired across the breathing cycle, sometimes with coached breathing) to characterize how much a target moves. Based on that motion, the team selects a motion management strategy: DIBH (deep inspiratory breath hold), abdominal compression, gated treatment (the beam only turns on during a specific part of the breathing cycle), or simple free-breathing.

Contouring and Target Volumes

After the simulation scan is imported by dosimetry (and fused/registered to other imaging such as MRI or PET if needed, using either rigid or deformable registration), the physician contours the structures that will guide the plan. A specific hierarchy of target volumes is used, and mixing these up is a common source of confusion:

  • GTV (gross tumor volume): the tumor you can actually see on imaging or exam.
  • CTV (clinical target volume): GTV plus a margin for suspected microscopic disease spread.
  • ITV (internal target volume): CTV plus a margin to account for internal organ motion (e.g., breathing).
  • PTV (planning target volume): ITV (or CTV) plus a further margin for daily setup uncertainty, this is the volume the plan is actually designed to cover.
  • OAR (organ at risk): a normal structure whose dose needs to be limited.
  • PRV (planning risk volume): an OAR plus a margin, analogous to how PTV relates to CTV, used to add a safety margin around critical normal structures.

Modalities and Techniques

The overall category of treatment is RT or XRT (radiotherapy), which splits into EBRT (external beam radiation therapy) and brachytherapy. Under EBRT you will see 2D, 3D-CRT, IMRT, VMAT, and SRS/SBRT: an escalating hierarchy of conformality and precision (see the Radiation Delivery & Technique doc for how each works), enabled at the hardware level by MLCs (multi-leaf collimators). Under brachytherapy you will see LDR and HDR (low- and high-dose-rate), with LDR classically associated with permanent radioactive "seeds."

Prescribing and Describing Dose

The Rx dose is the prescribed total dose. When a tumor bed needs extra dose beyond what surrounding tissue receives, this "boost" can be delivered in one of two ways: a sequential boost ("cone down"), where the larger volume is treated to an initial dose and then the field is shrunk to treat only the boost volume to the remaining dose in a separate second phase (e.g., 2 Gy/fraction × 25 fractions = 50 Gy, then 2 Gy/fraction × 5 more fractions = an additional 10 Gy boost, for 60 Gy total); or a simultaneous integrated boost (SIB), where both the larger volume and the boost volume are treated every day of a single phase, just at different dose-per-fraction levels (e.g., 2 Gy/fraction to the larger volume and 2.4 Gy/fraction to the boost volume, delivered together across the same 25 fractions).

Photon beams are described by their nominal energy in megavolts, written as 6X, 10X, 15X, 18X (i.e., 6 MV, 10 MV, etc.). A beam delivered without a flattening filter is called FFF (flattening filter free): used, for example, in SRS to increase dose rate. It is important to distinguish dose, measured in Gray (Gy), which is what gets prescribed, from the monitor unit (MU), which is the unit the machine itself uses internally to deliver that dose. Finally, a DVH (dose-volume histogram) is the standard graph used during plan review to show what percentage of a structure's volume receives at least a given dose, it is the tool used to check a plan against the dose constraints discussed elsewhere in this deck.

Image Guidance at Treatment Time

IGRT (image-guided radiotherapy) refers to imaging the patient immediately before (or during) each treatment to confirm positioning, using modalities such as MV or kV planar imaging, CBCT (cone-beam CT), MRI, fluoroscopy, and sometimes implanted fiducials (small markers placed to help localize a moving or hard-to-see target). CBCT is easily confused with a diagnostic FBCT (helical/"fan-beam" CT), but they serve different purposes: FBCT delivers a higher radiation dose, has better soft-tissue resolution, and takes longer, making it appropriate for diagnosis, while CBCT delivers much less dose, is faster, and is optimized for daily setup verification of a smaller area rather than diagnostic image quality.

Outcomes and Toxicity Grading

Two grading systems are used to standardize how treatment side effects are reported: RTOG grading (an older, radiation-specific toxicity scale) and CTCAE grading (Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, the current standard, more general oncology toxicity scale). Treatment success, on the other hand, is tracked with a family of oncologic outcome acronyms that are frequently confused with each other: OS (overall survival), PFS (progression-free survival), DFS (disease-free survival), EFS (event-free survival), and DMFS (distant metastasis-free survival): each defines a slightly different endpoint (whether death, any progression, any recurrence, a broader "event," or specifically distant spread counts against the outcome), so always check which one a study or note is actually reporting. QoL (quality of life) is tracked alongside these hard outcomes, since a treatment can extend survival while still meaningfully affecting how a patient feels day to day.

Clinical PearlWhen you see an unfamiliar acronym in a rad onc note, first ask which stage of the Sim → Planning → Plan Review → Treatment → Follow-up pathway it belongs to, most acronyms are specific to just one of those stages, and knowing the stage narrows down what the term could possibly mean even before you look it up.
